1/2 Thanks Gavin for an especially thoughtful exchange. I don't usually spend much time on social media but I wanted to engage here because it really brings out the heart of an important conversation. First, on regulation, I think that “either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely” is a false choice. I know that there’s a sort of Silicon Valley shorthand where regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power, but I’ve always found this to be an overly simplified picture of the world. Many people outside this bubble think of regulation as something that constrains corporate power and benefits ordinary people. I don’t necessarily agree with that perspective either, rather I think it’s complicated and really depends on what the “regulation” consists of. But in particular I think that those in the “regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power” frame often underrate the decentralizing power of objective and fair institutional processes. A crude analogy is that the formal court system can sometimes feel stuffy and elitist, but it does a much better job of defending the rights of vulnerable individuals than the alternative, mob justice. At their best, institutions can vest power in ideas rather than people, and thereby decentralize that power. This is why Anthropic has always made its policy proposals very carefully. We try very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors. California’s SB53 (which we supported), and even the much-maligned SB 1047 (which we were ambivalent on), completely exempt any company below a certain amount of revenue or model training costs from being covered at all (it was $500M for SB 53, lower for 1047 but we objected to that). More recently the testing process we’ve advocated for at CAISI and the White House involves more rigorous tests for frontier models than off-frontier models — something that differentially advantages challengers. Similarly, the “Pacing the Frontier” letter envisions (or at least Anthropic’s preferred implementation of it envisions) modulating the pace of the very best models while not constraining those who are catching up. This hurts the business interests of the frontier labs and helps challengers, including open-weights! Overall my view is that AI is *structurally* a technology that tends to concentrate power, for reasons that have nothing to do with regulation (more to do with the extreme implications of the scaling laws). Open-weights do help some with this but are nowhere near a sufficient solution because they simply shift the concentration somewhat to those with the most compute and chips (which are roughly the frontier labs plus maybe hardware providers). By contrast I think the right “rules of the road” can simultaneously (a) address AI’s cyber/bio/alignment risks, (b) institutionally constrain the power of the frontier AI companies, and (c) leave room for open-weights models while also addressing the specific risks that they bring. BTW I do not think that the events of the last few months have “failed to result in [my] preferred regulatory path”. The approach that the Trump administration is reported to be taking — pre-deployment testing for frontier models, and also testing of open-weights models when they get closer to the frontier — is one that I am very supportive of, though of course I have to see the details to be sure. I am also supportive of Demis Hassabis’ ideas around a FINRA-like entity. This contrasts with six months ago when most of the industry was still pushing for preemption of all state regulation and no apparent federal approach either. Gavin Baker (@GavinSBaker) Sholto, thank you for setting the record straight. Larger issue is that multiple very serious people in Silicon Valley have heard some variation of this and believe it to be true. And the reason it is believable to so many is that it is consistent with Dario’s public messaging and what he outlined in the essay you shared: this technology *might* be dangerous for humans in multiple ways, could lead to extreme concentration of economic power (as outlined in the essay) and therefore needs to be regulated thoughtfully. I agree with the potential risks and I believe Dario makes all of these arguments in good faith. As discussed on the pod, if one agrees that AI *might* be dangerous, there are two ways to address this potential risk. Either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely. Essentially boils down to whether one believes AI is too dangerous to concentrate or too dangerous to distribute. There are reasonable arguments on both sides, but I profoundly agree with Zuckerberg’s statement that: “The notion that AI is so dangerous that the only safe path is an extreme concentration of power seems inherently problematic. Historically, hoping that an absolute power will benevolently provide for humanity if sufficiently enlightened has not led to safe or positive outcomes.” And as Dario says in the aforementioned essay, “some may object that we can simply keep AIs in check with a balance of power between many AI systems, as we do with humans.” I believe this is the best path forward: I want as many AIs as possible to maximize the odds that one shares my own particular values. And as Dario notes, no human has ever been able to take over the world. At this point, I think safe to say that Dario has lost the argument. His messaging has failed to result in his preferred regulatory path. The fact that the only solution to the recent incident where an unreleased advanced OpenAI model hacked Hugging Face was an open-source model likely ended any chance of strict near-term regulation. Essentially every major company other than Anthropic has signed Jensen’s letter. However, Dario’s messaging has been massively helpful to efforts to ban datacenters here in America. I suspect we will see anti-datacenter advocacy groups runnings ads using clips of Dario warning about how dangerous AI could be for humans. His good faith efforts in favor of regulation are now increasing the odds that AI will not be beneficial for Americans and humans everywhere. I believe that there is a reasonable chance AI might help us cure most forms of disease such that we have extended lifespans and can enjoy these long lives in an abundant Star Trek like future. That is the future that I want and I think Dario is decreasing the odds of that future at this point. He is about to be the CEO of one of the most important public companies in the world and given that the pro-regulatory effort has failed (at least for now), I respectfully think he should make an effort to be a more positive advocate for his own industry. And if I am wrong and we do need to regulate this technology, he will be a more effective advocate for this in the future having been open-minded to the alternative. And for the sake of clarity and as I outlined on the pod, I think Anthropic has deep competitive advantages and is an amazing company. Ironically, the main risk I saw to Anthropic a few months ago was nationalization as a result of Dario’s own rhetoric and behavior. — http://shitter.thepixora.com/GavinSBaker/status/2088611616577253502#m

2/2 Second, on the messaging around AI. I do not agree that my messaging has been disproportionately negative. In fact it has been about equally balanced between risks and benefits: I’ve written one major essay about each, and even in interviews where I discuss the risks, I make sure to frequently mention the incredible benefits as well as proposing possible solutions to the risks (short clips from my interviews that end up on social media tend to be disproportionately negative, as that gets clicks). In fact, I wrote Machines of Loving Grace because I didn’t feel the AI industry was painting an inspiring enough picture of how the technology could radically transform the world for the better. The bulk of the essay is devoted to refuting skepticism of AI’s potential in health and biology, and showing why I think it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!). And, if you read my most recent essay (Policy on the AI Exponential), I discuss concrete proposals for how to streamline the FDA process to make sure the deluge of AI-accelerated drugs isn’t slowed down by the regulatory process. I feel the urgency here: I lost my father to Hepatitis C only a few years before the development of direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir), which cure 95% of patients and probably would have cured him. I do agree that the public has a negative view of AI (and that this is a big problem), but I don’t think it is primarily caused by me or any other AI leader warning about AI’s risks. I think it is fundamentally a crisis of trust. I think that ordinary people don’t trust companies, governments, or the tech industry and always suspect that we are cooking up some new way to screw them over. The causes of this go back decades and AI is just the latest iteration of it. I don’t think that a glitzy marketing campaign with a positive spin (which some have advocated that Anthropic do) is the way to win back that trust — at this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliche than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive. The thing that will work is *actually curing cancer*. I think by far the most accurate criticism of AI companies including Anthropic is that we haven’t yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world. That is totally on us, and I think it’s the criticism you should be making, instead of all this stuff about messaging and marketing. We are however doing our best to fix this: Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine, and we hope to have incredible results in the coming years and some early glimmers in the coming months. When we’ve actually accomplished something real, the whole world will hear about it, as loudly as possible, you have my word on that. But until then I don’t want to make empty promises, and in the meantime I feel compelled to speak honestly about the very real risks of AI and how to address them. Honesty is the right thing on the merits, and in terms of public credibility and trust it is no worse than, and may in fact be better than, an approach that ignores or distracts from risks which people instinctively understand are real.

In addition to transparency, I now believe frontier models should face mandatory third-party testing for cyber, bio, and autonomy risks—with the power to block or revoke deployment of models that pose catastrophic risk.

Alongside it, Anthropic is releasing a proposal for how governments can address the risks posed by frontier AI and a policy framework for job displacement, for which we intend to provide substantial financial backing. anthropic.com/policy-on-the-… Link Policy on the AI Exponential We are sharing two policy proposals to prepare for AI progress: Our Advanced AI Framework and our Economic Policy Framework. anthropic.com

processed.summary: Aujourd'hui, le monde de l'IA a été marqué par d'intenses discussions sur la sécurité et la régulation, avec des leaders comme Dario Amodei qui appellent à ralentir le développement des IA les plus avancées pour mieux en maîtriser les risques. Des réflexions profondes ont émergé sur l'avenir du travail avec l'IA et la manière dont les développeurs devront s'adapter, mettant l'accent sur la compréhension plutôt que sur la simple exécution de code. Enfin, des annonces de progrès technologiques et de nouvelles initiatives pour rendre l'IA plus transparente et accessible ont offert un aperçu des opportunités et des défis qui nous attendent.

glossaire.definition: Désigne les modèles d'intelligence artificielle les plus avancés et les plus puissants du moment, souvent développés par de grandes entreprises.
Concept selon lequel une IA doit se comporter de manière à respecter les valeurs et les intentions humaines, sans dérives inattendues ou dangereuses.
Un grand modèle de langage est une intelligence artificielle entraînée sur d'énormes quantités de texte pour comprendre, générer et répondre à des questions en langage naturel.

Caractérise un modèle d'IA dont les paramètres internes (les 'poids' qui définissent son fonctionnement) sont rendus publics, permettant à quiconque de l'étudier, de l'améliorer ou de l'utiliser librement.
Fait référence à une période future où les systèmes d'IA ne se contenteront plus de répondre à des requêtes, mais pourront agir de manière autonome pour accomplir des objectifs complexes.
Des mécanismes de sécurité intégrés dans les systèmes d'IA pour limiter leurs comportements indésirables ou dangereux et s'assurer qu'ils restent dans des limites acceptables.

category_summaries.actu: Les actualités du jour mettent en lumière les engagements d'Anthropic pour des audits de sécurité tiers et des propositions de régulation, ainsi que les avancées rapides des modèles comme Grok d'Elon Musk. On note aussi l'annonce de l'ARC Prize 2026, un concours stimulant l'innovation en IA générale, et des nouvelles concernant Neuralink.
category_summaries.tips: Pour les débutants, il est essentiel de retenir que l'IA peut aider à coder, mais ne doit jamais remplacer la compréhension humaine, selon François Chollet. De plus, la plateforme Replit est présentée comme un excellent outil pour développer rapidement des projets, y compris des jeux, en quelques minutes.
category_summaries.idees: Le débat autour de l'IA est très riche, notamment sur la nécessité de la réguler pour éviter la concentration de pouvoir et les risques de 'désalignement' (où l'IA pourrait mentir sur ses intentions). Des experts comme Jeremy Howard remettent en question certaines peurs exagérées, tandis que d'autres s'interrogent sur l'impact de l'IA sur l'ingénierie logicielle et le rôle futur des développeurs.
category_summaries.outils: Plusieurs initiatives visent à rendre l'IA plus sûre et accessible. L'Open Alignment Initiative propose de travailler sur l'alignement en toute transparence. La plateforme Replit est mise en avant comme un environnement de développement qui permet de transformer rapidement des idées en projets fonctionnels, comme le montre un exemple de succès entrepreneurial.

idees.text_fr: 1/2 Merci Gavin pour cet échange particulièrement réfléchi. Je ne passe généralement pas beaucoup de temps sur les réseaux sociaux, mais je voulais m'engager ici car cela met vraiment en lumière le cœur d'une conversation importante. Premièrement, sur la régulation, je pense que 'soit la concentrer entre les mains de quelques entreprises et politiciens choisis via la régulation, soit la distribuer largement' est un faux dilemme. Je sais qu'il existe une sorte de raccourci dans la Silicon Valley où régulation = capture réglementaire = concentration du pouvoir, mais j'ai toujours trouvé que c'était une image trop simplifiée du monde. Beaucoup de gens en dehors de cette bulle considèrent la régulation comme quelque chose qui contraint le pouvoir des entreprises et profite aux gens ordinaires. Je ne suis pas nécessairement d'accord avec cette perspective non plus, je pense plutôt que c'est compliqué et que cela dépend vraiment de ce en quoi consiste la 'régulation'. Mais en particulier, je pense que ceux qui sont dans le cadre 'régulation = capture réglementaire = concentration du pouvoir' sous-estiment souvent le pouvoir de décentralisation des processus institutionnels objectifs et équitables. Une analogie grossière est que le système judiciaire formel peut parfois sembler pompeux et élitiste, mais il fait un bien meilleur travail de défense des droits des individus vulnérables que l'alternative, la justice populaire. Au mieux, les institutions peuvent investir le pouvoir dans les idées plutôt que dans les personnes, et ainsi décentraliser ce pouvoir. C'est pourquoi Anthropic a toujours élaboré ses propositions politiques très soigneusement. Nous nous efforçons de faire des propositions qui désavantagent (ralentissent) les entreprises d'IA de pointe tout en *avantageant* les petits concurrents. La SB53 de Californie (que nous avons soutenue), et même la très décriée SB 1047 (sur laquelle nous étions ambivalents), exemptent complètement toute entreprise en dessous d'un certain montant de revenus ou de coûts d'entraînement de modèles d'être couverte (c'était 500 millions de dollars pour la SB 53, moins pour la 1047 mais nous nous y sommes opposés). Plus récemment, le processus de test que nous avons préconisé chez CAISI et la Maison Blanche implique des tests plus rigoureux pour les modèles de pointe que pour les modèles hors pointe — quelque chose qui avantage différemment les challengers. De même, la lettre 'Pacing the Frontier' envisage (ou du moins l'implémentation préférée d'Anthropic l'envisage) de moduler le rythme des meilleurs modèles sans contraindre ceux qui sont en train de rattraper leur retard. Cela nuit aux intérêts commerciaux des laboratoires de pointe et aide les challengers, y compris les modèles à poids ouverts ! Globalement, mon point de vue est que l'IA est *structurellement* une technologie qui tend à concentrer le pouvoir, pour des raisons qui n'ont rien à voir avec la régulation (plus à voir avec les implications extrêmes des lois d'échelle). Les poids ouverts aident un peu à cela mais sont loin d'être une solution suffisante car ils ne font que déplacer la concentration vers ceux qui ont le plus de calcul et de puces (qui sont grosso modo les laboratoires de pointe plus peut-être les fournisseurs de matériel). Par contraste, je pense que les bonnes 'règles du jeu' peuvent simultanément (a) aborder les risques cyber/bio/d'alignement de l'IA, (b) contraindre institutionnellement le pouvoir des entreprises d'IA de pointe, et (c) laisser de la place aux modèles à poids ouverts tout en abordant les risques spécifiques qu'ils apportent. D'ailleurs, je ne pense pas que les événements des derniers mois 'n'aient pas abouti à [ma] voie réglementaire préférée'. L'approche que l'administration Trump serait en train d'adopter — des tests avant déploiement pour les modèles de pointe, et aussi des tests des modèles à poids ouverts lorsqu'ils se rapprochent de la pointe — est une approche que je soutiens fortement, même si bien sûr je dois en voir les détails pour en être sûr. Je soutiens également les idées de Demis Hassabis concernant une entité de type FINRA. Cela contraste avec il y a six mois où la plupart de l'industrie poussait encore à la préemption de toute régulation étatique et à aucune approche fédérale apparente non plus. Gavin Baker (@GavinSBaker) Sholto, merci d'avoir remis les pendules à l'heure. Le problème plus vaste est que plusieurs personnes très sérieuses dans la Silicon Valley ont entendu une variante de cela et croient que c'est vrai. Et la raison pour laquelle c'est crédible pour tant de gens est que c'est cohérent avec le message public de Dario et ce qu'il a exposé dans l'essai que vous avez partagé : cette technologie *pourrait* être dangereuse pour les humains de multiples façons, pourrait conduire à une concentration extrême du pouvoir économique (as outlined in the essay) et donc needs to be regulated thoughtfully. I agree with the potential risks and I believe Dario makes all of these arguments in good faith. As discussed on the pod, if one agrees that AI *might* be dangerous, there are two ways to address this potential risk. Either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely. Essentially boils down to whether one believes AI is too dangerous to concentrate or too dangerous to distribute. There are reasonable arguments on both sides, but I profoundly agree with Zuckerberg’s statement that: “The notion that AI is so dangerous that the only safe path is an extreme concentration of power seems inherently problematic. Historically, hoping that an absolute power will benevolently provide for humanity if sufficiently enlightened has not led to safe or positive outcomes.” And as Dario says in the aforementioned essay, “some may object that we can simply keep AIs in check with a balance of power between many AI systems, as we do with humans.” I believe this is the best path forward: I want as many AIs as possible to maximize the odds that one shares my own particular values. And as Dario notes, no human has ever been able to take over the world. At this point, I think safe to say that Dario has lost the argument. His messaging has failed to result in his preferred regulatory path. The fact that the only solution to the recent incident where an unreleased advanced OpenAI model hacked Hugging Face was an open-source model likely ended any chance of strict near-term regulation. Essentially every major company other than Anthropic has signed Jensen’s letter. However, Dario’s messaging has been massively helpful to efforts to ban datacenters here in America. I suspect we will see anti-datacenter advocacy groups runnings ads using clips of Dario warning about how dangerous AI could be for humans. His good faith efforts in favor of regulation are now increasing the odds that AI will not be beneficial for Americans and humans everywhere. I believe that there is a reasonable chance AI might help us cure most forms of disease such that we have extended lifespans and can enjoy these long lives in an abundant Star Trek like future. That is the future that I want and I think Dario is decreasing the odds of that future at this point. He is about to be the CEO of one of the most important public companies in the world and given that the pro-regulatory effort has failed (at least for now), I respectfully think he should make an effort to be a more positive advocate for his own industry. And if I am wrong and we do need to regulate this technology, he will be a more effective advocate for this in the future having been open-minded to the alternative. And for the sake of clarity and as I outlined on the pod, I think Anthropic has deep competitive advantages and is an amazing company. Ironically, the main risk I saw to Anthropic a few months ago was nationalization as a result of Dario’s own rhetoric and behavior.

idees.text_fr: 2/2 Deuxièmement, sur la communication autour de l'IA. Je ne suis pas d'accord pour dire que mon message a été disproportionnellement négatif. En fait, il a été à peu près également équilibré entre les risques et les avantages : j'ai écrit un essai majeur sur chacun, et même dans les interviews où je discute des risques, je m'assure de mentionner fréquemment les incroyables avantages ainsi que de proposer des solutions possibles aux risques (les extraits courts de mes interviews qui se retrouvent sur les réseaux sociaux ont tendance à être disproportionnellement négatifs, car cela génère des clics). En fait, j'ai écrit 'Machines of Loving Grace' parce que je ne sentais pas que l'industrie de l'IA dépeignait une image suffisamment inspirante de la façon dont la technologie pourrait transformer radicalement le monde pour le mieux. L'essentiel de l'essai est consacré à réfuter le scepticisme quant au potentiel de l'IA dans la santé et la biologie, et à montrer pourquoi je pense qu'il sera réellement possible de guérir la plupart des maladies humaines en environ 5 à 10 ans, aussi fou que cela puisse paraître aux gens ordinaires et, franchement, aux biologistes aussi (j'en étais un !). Et, si vous lisez mon essai le plus récent ('Policy on the AI Exponential'), je discute de propositions concrètes pour rationaliser le processus de la FDA afin de s'assurer que le déluge de médicaments accélérés par l'IA ne soit pas ralenti par le processus réglementaire. Je ressens l'urgence ici : j'ai perdu mon père à cause de l'hépatite C quelques années seulement avant le développement des antiviraux à action directe (sofosbuvir), qui guérissent 95% des patients et l'auraient probablement guéri. Je suis d'accord pour dire que le public a une opinion négative de l'IA (et que c'est un gros problème), mais je ne pense pas que cela soit principalement causé par moi ou tout autre leader de l'IA qui alerte sur les risques de l'IA. Je pense que c'est fondamentalement une crise de confiance. Je pense que les gens ordinaires ne font pas confiance aux entreprises, aux gouvernements ou à l'industrie technologique et soupçonnent toujours que nous préparons une nouvelle façon de les arnaquer. Les causes de cela remontent à des décennies et l'IA n'en est que la dernière itération. Je ne pense pas qu'une campagne de marketing tape-à-l'œil avec une tournure positive (que certains ont préconisé à Anthropic de faire) soit le moyen de regagner cette confiance — à ce stade, dire que l'IA va guérir le cancer est plus un cliché qu'une source d'inspiration, et la plupart des gens pensent que c'est trompeur. Ce qui fonctionnera, c'est de *réellement guérir le cancer*. Je pense que la critique la plus juste des entreprises d'IA, y compris Anthropic, est que nous n'avons pas encore tenu nos grandes promesses de bénéficier au monde. C'est entièrement de notre faute, et je pense que c'est la critique que vous devriez faire, au lieu de tout ce bla-bla sur la communication et le marketing. Nous faisons cependant de notre mieux pour y remédier : Anthropic intensifie très rapidement ses efforts en biologie et en médecine, et nous espérons avoir des résultats incroyables dans les années à venir et quelques premiers aperçus dans les mois à venir. Lorsque nous aurons réellement accompli quelque chose de concret, le monde entier en entendra parler, aussi fort que possible, je vous donne ma parole là-dessus. Mais d'ici là, je ne veux pas faire de fausses promesses, et en attendant, je me sens obligé de parler honnêtement des risques très réels de l'IA et de la façon de les aborder. L'honnêteté est la bonne chose sur le fond, et en termes de crédibilité et de confiance du public, ce n'est pas pire que, et peut même être mieux que, une approche qui ignore ou détourne l'attention des risques qui people instinctively understand are real.
idees.text_original: 2/2 Second, on the messaging around AI. I do not agree that my messaging has been disproportionately negative. In fact it has been about equally balanced between risks and benefits: I’ve written one major essay about each, and even in interviews where I discuss the risks, I make sure to frequently mention the incredible benefits as well as proposing possible solutions to the risks (short clips from my interviews that end up on social media tend to be disproportionately negative, as that gets clicks). In fact, I wrote Machines of Loving Grace because I didn’t feel the AI industry was painting an inspiring enough picture of how the technology could radically transform the world for the better. The bulk of the essay is devoted to refuting skepticism of AI’s potential in health and biology, and showing why I think it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!). And, if you read my most recent essay (Policy on the AI Exponential), I discuss concrete proposals for how to streamline the FDA process to make sure the deluge of AI-accelerated drugs isn’t slowed down by the regulatory process. I feel the urgency here: I lost my father to Hepatitis C only a few years before the development of direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir), which cure 95% of patients and probably would have cured him. I do agree that the public has a negative view of AI (and that this is a big problem), but I don’t think it is primarily caused by me or any other AI leader warning about AI’s risks. I think it is fundamentally a crisis of trust. I think that ordinary people don’t trust companies, governments, or the tech industry and always suspect that we are cooking up some new way to screw them over. The causes of this go back decades and AI is just the latest iteration of it. I don’t think that a glitzy marketing campaign with a positive spin (which some have advocated that Anthropic do) is the way to win back that trust — at this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliche than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive. The thing that will work is *actually curing cancer*. I think by far the most accurate criticism of AI companies including Anthropic is that we haven’t yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world. That is totally on us, and I think it’s the criticism you should be making, instead of all this stuff about messaging and marketing. We are however doing our best to fix this: Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine, and we hope to have incredible results in the coming years and some early glimmers in the coming months. When we’ve actually accomplished something real, the whole world will hear about it, as loudly as possible, you have my word on that. But until then I don’t want to make empty promises, and in the meantime I feel compelled to speak honestly about the very real risks of AI and how to address them. Honesty is the right thing on the merits, and in terms of public credibility and trust it is no worse than, and may in fact be better than, an approach that ignores or distracts from risks which people instinctively understand are real.
